claim: Loss of Ppz phosphatase activity leads to defects in ubiquitin homeostasis.
source: We find that loss of Ppz phosphatase activity leads to defects in ubiquitin homeostasis that are at least partially attributable to elevated levels of Ser57 phosphorylated ubiquitin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing ubiquitin deficiency in ppz mutants (Figure 1B-D) and elevated Ser57 phosphorylation (Figure 1A).

claim: Elevated levels of Ser57 phosphorylated ubiquitin are at least partially responsible for ubiquitin homeostasis defects in ppz mutants.
source: We find that loss of Ppz phosphatase activity leads to defects in ubiquitin homeostasis that are at least partially attributable to elevated levels of Ser57 phosphorylated ubiquitin.
evidence: Supported by data showing that Ser57Ala mutation partially suppresses ubiquitin deficiency in ppz mutants (Figure 2A-B).

claim: Phosphomimetic mutation at the Ser57 position of ubiquitin confers increased rates of endocytic trafficking.
source: Phosphomimetic mutation at the Ser57 position of ubiquitin conferred increased rates of endocytic trafficking and ubiquitin turnover.
evidence: Supported by canavanine resistance assays (Figure 4A-B) and Mup1-pHluorin trafficking experiments (Figure 4C-D).

claim: Phosphomimetic mutation at the Ser57 position of ubiquitin confers increased rates of ubiquitin turnover.
source: Phosphomimetic mutation at the Ser57 position of ubiquitin conferred increased rates of endocytic trafficking and ubiquitin turnover.
evidence: Supported by ubiquitin half-life measurements showing faster degradation of Ser57Asp ubiquitin (Figure 3A-D).

claim: Ser57 phosphorylation phenotypes are associated with bypass of recognition by endosome-localized deubiquitylases.
source: These phenotypes are associated with bypass of recognition by endosome-localized deubiquitylases - including Doa4 which is critical for regulation of ubiquitin recycling.
evidence: Supported by in vitro deubiquitylation assays showing reduced Doa4 activity toward Ser57Asp ubiquitin (Figure 6A-E) and bypass of artificial DUB checkpoint (Figure 5B-D).

claim: Doa4 is critical for regulation of ubiquitin recycling.
source: These phenotypes are associated with bypass of recognition by endosome-localized deubiquitylases - including Doa4 which is critical for regulation of ubiquitin recycling.
evidence: Supported by established literature and data showing increased ubiquitin turnover in doa4 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: Ubiquitin homeostasis is significantly impacted by the rate of ubiquitin flux through the endocytic pathway.
source: Thus, ubiquitin homeostasis is significantly impacted by the rate of ubiquitin flux through the endocytic pathway and by signaling pathways that converge on ubiquitin itself to determine whether it is recycled or degraded in the vacuole.
evidence: Supported by data showing that ESCRT pathway mutations stabilize ubiquitin (Figure 7C-D) and ubiquitin accumulates in E-compartments of snf7 mutants (Figure 7E).

claim: Signaling pathways converge on ubiquitin itself to determine whether it is recycled or degraded in the vacuole.
source: Thus, ubiquitin homeostasis is significantly impacted by the rate of ubiquitin flux through the endocytic pathway and by signaling pathways that converge on ubiquitin itself to determine whether it is recycled or degraded in the vacuole.
evidence: Supported by data showing Ser57 phosphorylation affects ubiquitin fate and Ppz phosphatases regulate this modification.

claim: Many human diseases, particularly neurodegenerative disorders, are associated with diminished function of the ubiquitin-proteasome system and altered ubiquitin homeostasis.
source: There is mounting evidence that many human diseases – particularly diseases related to protein misfolding and aggregation such as neurodegenerative disorders - are associated with diminished function of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) and altered ubiquitin homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: Protein aggregates in neurodegenerative disorders tend to accumulate ubiquitin conjugated to aggregated proteins.
source: In general, protein aggregates found in neurodegenerative disorders (Lewy bodies in Parkinson's disease, neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease, etc.) tend to accumulate ubiquitin, which is conjugated to aggregated proteins (Dawson and Dawson, 2003; Hallengren et al., 2013; Upadhya and Hegde, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dysregulation of ubiquitin homeostasis has been observed in mouse models of Huntington's disease.
source: Dysregulation of ubiquitin homeostasis has been observed in mouse models of Huntington's disease (Bennett et al., 2007), spinal muscular atrophy (Wishart et al., 2014), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Gilchrist et al., 2005; Hallengren et al., 2013), and Alzheimer's disease (Lam et al., 2000; Upadhya and Hegde, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bennett et al., 2007.

claim: Dysregulation of ubiquitin homeostasis has been observed in mouse models of spinal muscular atrophy.
source: Dysregulation of ubiquitin homeostasis has been observed in mouse models of Huntington's disease (Bennett et al., 2007), spinal muscular atrophy (Wishart et al., 2014), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Gilchrist et al., 2005; Hallengren et al., 2013), and Alzheimer's disease (Lam et al., 2000; Upadhya and Hegde, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wishart et al., 2014.

claim: Dysregulation of ubiquitin homeostasis has been observed in mouse models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: Dysregulation of ubiquitin homeostasis has been observed in mouse models of Huntington's disease (Bennett et al., 2007), spinal muscular atrophy (Wishart et al., 2014), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Gilchrist et al., 2005; Hallengren et al., 2013), and Alzheimer's disease (Lam et al., 2000; Upadhya and Hegde, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gilchrist et al., 2005 and Hallengren et al., 2013.

claim: Dysregulation of ubiquitin homeostasis has been observed in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Dysregulation of ubiquitin homeostasis has been observed in mouse models of Huntington's disease (Bennett et al., 2007), spinal muscular atrophy (Wishart et al., 2014), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Gilchrist et al., 2005; Hallengren et al., 2013), and Alzheimer's disease (Lam et al., 2000; Upadhya and Hegde, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lam et al., 2000 and Upadhya and Hegde, 2007.

claim: Restoring ubiquitin levels and UPS activity has been proposed as a potential therapeutic strategy for neurodegeneration.
source: Given the emerging consensus that dysregulation of ubiquitin homeostasis and UPS activity is a key feature of neurodegeneration, some have proposed restoring ubiquitin levels and UPS activity as a potential therapeutic strategy (Chen et al., 2011; Chou and Deshaies, 2011; Deshaies, 2009; Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature proposing this strategy.

claim: Very little is known about regulation of ubiquitin homeostasis in physiological conditions, during cellular aging, in response to cellular stress, or in states of disease.
source: However, very little is known about regulation of ubiquitin homeostasis in physiological conditions, during cellular aging, in response to cellular stress, or in states of disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In yeast and mammalian cells, ubiquitin is synthesized from multiple genes encoding ubiquitin precursor proteins.
source: In yeast and mammalian cells, ubiquitin is synthesized from multiple (usually four) genes which encode ubiquitin precursor proteins consisting of either a single ubiquitin protein fused to a ribosomal protein subunit (Finley et al., 1989; Ozkaynak et al., 1987) or head-to-tail ubiquitin repeats (linear polymers) (Finley et al., 1987; Ryu et al., 2008a; Ryu et al., 2007; Ryu et al., 2008b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ubiquitin genes encode either a single ubiquitin protein fused to a ribosomal protein subunit or head-to-tail ubiquitin repeats.
source: In yeast and mammalian cells, ubiquitin is synthesized from multiple (usually four) genes which encode ubiquitin precursor proteins consisting of either a single ubiquitin protein fused to a ribosomal protein subunit (Finley et al., 1989; Ozkaynak et al., 1987) or head-to-tail ubiquitin repeats (linear polymers) (Finley et al., 1987; Ryu et al., 2008a; Ryu et al., 2007; Ryu et al., 2008b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Encoding ubiquitin as a fusion protein to ribosomal subunits allows cells to couple ubiquitin synthesis and ribosome biogenesis in nutrient-rich conditions.
source: Encoding ubiquitin as a fusion protein to ribosomal subunits allows cells to couple ubiquitin synthesis and ribosome biogenesis in nutrient-rich conditions that support protein translation and cellular growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of ubiquitin genes and cellular biology.

claim: Deubiquitylating enzymes that associate with protein degradation machinery tend to mediate recycling of ubiquitin.
source: Deubiquitylating enzymes (DUBs) that associate with protein degradation machinery (the proteasome and ESCRT machinery for soluble and membrane proteins, respectively) tend to mediate recycling of ubiquitin, and mutation of these DUBs leads to ubiquitin deficiency (Anderson et al., 2005; Hallengren et al., 2013; Leggett et al., 2002; Swaminathan et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mutation of DUBs that associate with protein degradation machinery leads to ubiquitin deficiency.
source: Deubiquitylating enzymes (DUBs) that associate with protein degradation machinery (the proteasome and ESCRT machinery for soluble and membrane proteins, respectively) tend to mediate recycling of ubiquitin, and mutation of these DUBs leads to ubiquitin deficiency (Anderson et al., 2005; Hallengren et al., 2013; Leggett et al., 2002; Swaminathan et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Doa4 is a yeast endosomal DUB that associates with the ESCRT machinery and recycles ubiquitin prior to membrane protein degradation.
source: In particular, Doa4 – a yeast endosomal DUB that associates with the ESCRT machinery and recycles ubiquitin prior to membrane protein degradation – has a critical role in both vacuolar trafficking and management of cellular ubiquitin levels.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: Doa4 has a critical role in both vacuolar trafficking and management of cellular ubiquitin levels.
source: In particular, Doa4 – a yeast endosomal DUB that associates with the ESCRT machinery and recycles ubiquitin prior to membrane protein degradation – has a critical role in both vacuolar trafficking and management of cellular ubiquitin levels.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and data in this study.

claim: doa4 mutant cells exhibit ubiquitin deficiency and vacuolar trafficking defects.
source: More specifically, doa4 mutant cells exhibit ubiquitin deficiency and vacuolar trafficking defects (Amerik et al., 2000; Kimura et al., 2009; Swaminathan et al., 1999), underscoring how trafficking along the endocytic route and the management of cellular ubiquitin levels are coupled.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Trafficking along the endocytic route and the management of cellular ubiquitin levels are coupled.
source: More specifically, doa4 mutant cells exhibit ubiquitin deficiency and vacuolar trafficking defects (Amerik et al., 2000; Kimura et al., 2009; Swaminathan et al., 1999), underscoring how trafficking along the endocytic route and the management of cellular ubiquitin levels are coupled.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the doa4 mutant phenotypes.

claim: Ubiquitin can polymerize at any of seven internal lysines or the N-terminus leading to chains of different linkage types.
source: The complexity of the ubiquitin code is underscored by the fact that ubiquitin can polymerize at any of seven internal lysines (or the N-terminus) leading to chains of different linkage types, each with a unique structure that can be interpreted differently, and that mixed-linkage or branched chains are also possible.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the ubiquitin field.

claim: Each ubiquitin chain linkage type has a unique structure that can be interpreted differently.
source: The complexity of the ubiquitin code is underscored by the fact that ubiquitin can polymerize at any of seven internal lysines (or the N-terminus) leading to chains of different linkage types, each with a unique structure that can be interpreted differently, and that mixed-linkage or branched chains are also possible.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the ubiquitin field.

claim: Mixed-linkage or branched ubiquitin chains are possible.
source: The complexity of the ubiquitin code is underscored by the fact that ubiquitin can polymerize at any of seven internal lysines (or the N-terminus) leading to chains of different linkage types, each with a unique structure that can be interpreted differently, and that mixed-linkage or branched chains are also possible.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the ubiquitin field.

claim: Post-translational modifications of ubiquitin (other than polymerization) can alter its function.
source: More recent work has also led to a consensus that post-translational modifications of ubiquitin (other than polymerization) can alter its function (Herhaus and Dikic, 2015; Zheng and Hunter, 2014) - making the ubiquitin code as we know it even more complex than previously appreciated.
evidence: Supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: The E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin is activated by Ser65 phosphorylated ubiquitin.
source: For example, several groups have reported that the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin – mutations in which cause an autosomal recessive form of early onset Parkinson's disease – is activated by Ser65 phosphorylated ubiquitin (Kane et al., 2014; Kazlauskaite et al., 2014; Koyano et al., 2014; Ordureau et al., 2014; Wauer et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Mutations in Parkin cause an autosomal recessive form of early onset Parkinson's disease.
source: For example, several groups have reported that the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin – mutations in which cause an autosomal recessive form of early onset Parkinson's disease – is activated by Ser65 phosphorylated ubiquitin (Kane et al., 2014; Kazlauskaite et al., 2014; Koyano et al., 2014; Ordureau et al., 2014; Wauer et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the Parkinson's disease field.

claim: The Pink1-Parkin system is not conserved in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Despite the fact that the Pink1-Parkin system is not conserved in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Ser65 phosphorylation of ubiquitin has been detected in yeast and recent work suggests it may play a role in the oxidative stress response (Swaney et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast biology.

claim: Ser65 phosphorylation of ubiquitin has been detected in yeast.
source: Despite the fact that the Pink1-Parkin system is not conserved in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Ser65 phosphorylation of ubiquitin has been detected in yeast and recent work suggests it may play a role in the oxidative stress response (Swaney et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Swaney et al., 2015.

claim: Ser65 phosphorylation of ubiquitin may play a role in the oxidative stress response in yeast.
source: Despite the fact that the Pink1-Parkin system is not conserved in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Ser65 phosphorylation of ubiquitin has been detected in yeast and recent work suggests it may play a role in the oxidative stress response (Swaney et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Swaney et al., 2015.

claim: Ser65 phospho-regulation of ubiquitin is highly conserved across evolution.
source: These findings suggest that Ser65 phospho-regulation of ubiquitin is highly conserved across evolution and likely has functional significance beyond Pink1-Parkin-mediated mitophagy.
evidence: This is an inference based on detection of Ser65 phosphorylation in both yeast and mammals.

claim: Ser65 phospho-regulation of ubiquitin likely has functional significance beyond Pink1-Parkin-mediated mitophagy.
source: These findings suggest that Ser65 phospho-regulation of ubiquitin is highly conserved across evolution and likely has functional significance beyond Pink1-Parkin-mediated mitophagy.
evidence: This is speculation based on conservation and detection in yeast which lacks Pink1-Parkin.

claim: Phosphorylation at other sites on ubiquitin has been detected in yeast and mammalian cells.
source: Importantly, several other studies have reported evidence of phosphorylation at other sites on ubiquitin in yeast (Peng et al., 2003) and mammalian (Villén et al., 2007) cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Different phosphorylation events on ubiquitin impact the in vitro activities of specific E2-conjugating enzymes, E3 ubiquitin ligases, and deubiquitylases.
source: While biochemical analysis has revealed that different phosphorylation events on ubiquitin impact the in vitro activities of specific E2-conjugating enzymes, E3 ubiquitin ligases, and deubiquitylases (Huguenin-Dezot et al., 2016; Wauer et al., 2015b) the actual functional significance of these modifications remain to be elucidated.
evidence: Supported by citations to biochemical studies.

claim: The actual functional significance of ubiquitin phosphorylation modifications remains to be elucidated.
source: While biochemical analysis has revealed that different phosphorylation events on ubiquitin impact the in vitro activities of specific E2-conjugating enzymes, E3 ubiquitin ligases, and deubiquitylases (Huguenin-Dezot et al., 2016; Wauer et al., 2015b) the actual functional significance of these modifications remain to be elucidated.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Ppz1 and Ppz2 are a pair of highly similar yeast phosphatases (57% identical).
source: Here, we report that a pair of highly similar yeast phosphatases – Ppz1 and Ppz2 – are required for proper management of ubiquitin homeostasis in yeast.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these yeast proteins.

claim: Ppz1 and Ppz2 are required for proper management of ubiquitin homeostasis in yeast.
source: Here, we report that a pair of highly similar yeast phosphatases – Ppz1 and Ppz2 – are required for proper management of ubiquitin homeostasis in yeast.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing ubiquitin deficiency in ppz mutants (Figure 1B-D).

claim: ppz mutants exhibit elevated levels of Ser57 phosphorylated ubiquitin.
source: We show that ppz mutants exhibit elevated levels of Ser57 phosphorylated ubiquitin – suggesting that Ser57 phosphorylation of ubiquitin may be linked to the regulation of ubiquitin homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by phosphoproteomic analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and immunoblotting (Figure 1A).

claim: Ser57 phosphorylation of ubiquitin may be linked to the regulation of ubiquitin homeostasis.
source: We show that ppz mutants exhibit elevated levels of Ser57 phosphorylated ubiquitin – suggesting that Ser57 phosphorylation of ubiquitin may be linked to the regulation of ubiquitin homeostasis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the correlation between elevated Ser57 phosphorylation and ubiquitin deficiency in ppz mutants.

claim: Phosphomimetic mutations at the Ser57 position confer increased rate of ubiquitin degradation.
source: We show that phosphomimetic mutations at the Ser57 position confer increased rate of ubiquitin degradation and gain-of-function endocytic trafficking phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by ubiquitin half-life measurements (Figure 3A-D).

claim: Phosphomimetic mutations at the Ser57 position confer gain-of-function endocytic trafficking phenotypes.
source: We show that phosphomimetic mutations at the Ser57 position confer increased rate of ubiquitin degradation and gain-of-function endocytic trafficking phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by canavanine resistance assays (Figure 4A-B) and Mup1 trafficking experiments (Figure 4C-D).

claim: Ser57 phosphomimetic phenotypes are associated with resistance to removal by deubiquitylases on yeast endosomes.
source: Furthermore, we present evidence that these phenotypes are associated with resistance to removal by deubiquitylases on yeast endosomes, and that this pathway plays a significant role in the regulation of ubiquitin metabolism.
evidence: Supported by in vitro Doa4 assays (Figure 6A-E) and DUB bypass experiments (Figure 5B-D).

claim: The pathway involving endosomal deubiquitylases plays a significant role in the regulation of ubiquitin metabolism.
source: Furthermore, we present evidence that these phenotypes are associated with resistance to removal by deubiquitylases on yeast endosomes, and that this pathway plays a significant role in the regulation of ubiquitin metabolism.
evidence: Supported by data showing that ESCRT pathway mutations stabilize ubiquitin (Figure 7C-D).

claim: Ser57 phosphorylation of ubiquitin can function as a regulatory switch to control ubiquitin recycling along the endocytic route.
source: Based on these findings, we propose Ser57 phosphorylation of ubiquitin as a potential mechanism for deciding whether ubiquitin is recycled or degraded during multi-vesicular body (MVB) sorting on endosomes, thus contributing to the global regulation of ubiquitin levels in the cell.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Ser57 phosphorylation of ubiquitin contributes to the global regulation of ubiquitin levels in the cell.
source: Based on these findings, we propose Ser57 phosphorylation of ubiquitin as a potential mechanism for deciding whether ubiquitin is recycled or degraded during multi-vesicular body (MVB) sorting on endosomes, thus contributing to the global regulation of ubiquitin levels in the cell.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: SILAC-based quantitative analysis identified an ~3-fold increase in phosphorylation of ubiquitin at the Ser57 position in ppz mutants.
source: We identified several phosphorylation events elevated in ppz mutants, including an ~3-fold increase in the phosphorylation of ubiquitin at the Ser57 position (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative phosphoproteomic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phosphorylation of ubiquitin at the Ser57 position has been reported previously.
source: Phosphorylation of ubiquitin at the Ser57 position has been reported previously (Peng et al., 2003), although this serine is not required for the essential function of ubiquitin (Sloper-Mould et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ser57 is not required for the essential function of ubiquitin.
source: Phosphorylation of ubiquitin at the Ser57 position has been reported previously (Peng et al., 2003), although this serine is not required for the essential function of ubiquitin (Sloper-Mould et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sloper-Mould et al., 2001.

claim: Ubiquitin phosphorylated at the Ser57 position was detected by a phospho-specific antibody in yeast cell lysates.
source: Ubiquitin phosphorylated at the Ser57 position was also detected by a phospho-specific antibody capable of detecting Ser57 phosphorylated mono- and di-ubiquitin in yeast cell lysates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Elevated levels of Ser57 phosphorylated ubiquitin were detected with the phospho-specific antibody in ppz mutant cell lysates.
source: Consistent with the quantitative phosphoproteomic analysis, elevated levels of Ser57 phosphorylated ubiquitin were detected with the phospho-specific antibody in ppz mutant cell lysates (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ppz mutants exhibit mono-ubiquitin deficiency.
source: Immunoblotting analysis revealed that ppz mutants exhibit mono-ubiquitin and total ubiquitin deficiencies (Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3–4).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: ppz mutants exhibit total ubiquitin deficiency.
source: Immunoblotting analysis revealed that ppz mutants exhibit mono-ubiquitin and total ubiquitin deficiencies (Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3–4).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Addition of either PPZ1 or PPZ2 can complement the ubiquitin deficiency observed in ppz mutant cells.
source: Importantly, complementation analysis revealed that addition of either PPZ1 or PPZ2 could complement the ubiquitin deficiency observed in ppz mutant cells (Figure 1B–C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by complementation data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: An R451L catalytic dead mutant of Ppz1 is unable to complement the ubiquitin deficiency.
source: Furthermore, an R451L catalytic dead mutant of Ppz1 was unable to complement the ubiquitin deficiency (Figure 1B–C), indicating that Ppz1 phosphatase activity is critical for ubiquitin management.
evidence: Supported by complementation data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Ppz1 phosphatase activity is critical for ubiquitin management.
source: Furthermore, an R451L catalytic dead mutant of Ppz1 was unable to complement the ubiquitin deficiency (Figure 1B–C), indicating that Ppz1 phosphatase activity is critical for ubiquitin management.
evidence: This is an inference from the inability of the catalytic dead mutant to complement.

claim: Ubiquitin degradation occurs faster in ppz mutants.
source: To explore this possibility, we performed cycloheximide chase experiments and measured ubiquitin turnover in wild-type and ppz mutant cells, which revealed that ubiquitin degradation occurs faster in ppz mutants (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: This is the first example of a signaling protein required for proper regulation of ubiquitin homeostasis.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first example of a signaling protein required for proper regulation of ubiquitin homeostasis.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding.

claim: ppz mutants exhibit resistance to LiCl and MnCl2.
source: In the course of these experiments, we observed several ppz mutant phenotypes including resistance to LiCl and MnCl2 and hypersensitivity to KCl and caffeine (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: ppz mutants exhibit hypersensitivity to KCl and caffeine.
source: In the course of these experiments, we observed several ppz mutant phenotypes including resistance to LiCl and MnCl2 and hypersensitivity to KCl and caffeine (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Ubiquitin overexpression in ppz mutant cells suppresses resistance to LiCl and MnCl2 and hypersensitivity to KCl and caffeine.
source: Strikingly, we found that ubiquitin overexpression (driven by the ADH1 promoter) in ppz mutant cells suppressed these phenotypes (Figure 1G), indicating that these phenotypes are caused by ubiquitin deficiency.
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: ppz mutant phenotypes (LiCl resistance, MnCl2 resistance, KCl sensitivity, caffeine sensitivity) are caused by ubiquitin deficiency.
source: Strikingly, we found that ubiquitin overexpression (driven by the ADH1 promoter) in ppz mutant cells suppressed these phenotypes (Figure 1G), indicating that these phenotypes are caused by ubiquitin deficiency.
evidence: This is an inference from the suppression by ubiquitin overexpression.

claim: doa4 mutants exhibit phenotypes that can be rescued by ubiquitin supplementation.
source: Importantly, doa4 mutants – which are also ubiquitin deficient – similarly exhibit phenotypes that can be rescued by ubiquitin supplementation (Amerik et al., 2000; Swaminathan et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Expression of Ser57Ala mutant ubiquitin can partially suppress the ubiquitin deficiency observed in ppz mutant cells.
source: This analysis revealed that expression of Ser57Ala mutant ubiquitin could partially suppress the ubiquitin deficiency observed in ppz mutant cells (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Increased ubiquitin turnover in ppz mutant cells can be suppressed by expression of Ser57Ala mutant ubiquitin.
source: Consistent with prior results (Figure 1E and F), this analysis revealed that ubiquitin is degraded faster in ppz mutant cells (Figure 2D) but this increased ubiquitin turnover can be suppressed by expression of Ser57Ala mutant ubiquitin (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Expression of Ser57Ala mutant ubiquitin in ppz mutant cells partially suppresses MnCl2 resistance, KCl sensitivity, and caffeine sensitivity.
source: Specifically, we observed that expression of Ser57Ala mutant ubiquitin in ppz mutant cells partially suppressed MnCl2 resistance, KCl sensitivity, and caffeine sensitivity, although it had no affect on the LiCl resistance phenotype (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Expression of Ser57Ala mutant ubiquitin in ppz mutant cells has no effect on the LiCl resistance phenotype.
source: Specifically, we observed that expression of Ser57Ala mutant ubiquitin in ppz mutant cells partially suppressed MnCl2 resistance, KCl sensitivity, and caffeine sensitivity, although it had no affect on the LiCl resistance phenotype (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Elevated phosphorylation of ubiquitin at the Ser57 position contributes partially to the ubiquitin deficiency observed in ppz mutant cells.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that elevated phosphorylation of ubiquitin at the Ser57 position contributes partially to the ubiquitin deficiency observed in ppz mutant cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the partial suppression by Ser57Ala mutation.

claim: Ser57Ala ubiquitin turns over more slowly than wild-type ubiquitin.
source: We found that Ser57Ala ubiquitin turned over more slowly than wild-type ubiquitin, while Ser57Asp ubiquitin turned over faster than wild-type ubiquitin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitin half-life data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ser57Asp ubiquitin turns over faster than wild-type ubiquitin.
source: We found that Ser57Ala ubiquitin turned over more slowly than wild-type ubiquitin, while Ser57Asp ubiquitin turned over faster than wild-type ubiquitin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitin half-life data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ser57Asp ubiquitin exhibits a significantly shorter half-life than wildtype ubiquitin in a galactose induction/glucose repression system.
source: To explore this further, we measured ubiquitin half-life using a galactose induction/glucose repression system and found that Ser57Asp ubiquitin exhibits a significantly shorter half-life than wildtype (Figure 3A–D) while Ser57Ala ubiquitin exhibited a half-life equivalent to wild-type ubiquitin (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitin half-life data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: Ser57Ala ubiquitin exhibits a half-life equivalent to wild-type ubiquitin in a galactose induction/glucose repression system.
source: To explore this further, we measured ubiquitin half-life using a galactose induction/glucose repression system and found that Ser57Asp ubiquitin exhibits a significantly shorter half-life than wildtype (Figure 3A–D) while Ser57Ala ubiquitin exhibited a half-life equivalent to wild-type ubiquitin (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitin half-life data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mutations that prevent or mimic phosphorylation at Ser57 modulate ubiquitin turnover.
source: These data suggest that Ser57 phosphorylation may regulate ubiquitin turnover in the cell since mutations that prevent or mimic phosphorylation modulate ubiquitin turnover.
evidence: This is an inference from the differential turnover rates of Ser57Ala and Ser57Asp ubiquitin.

claim: Ser57 phosphorylation may regulate ubiquitin turnover in the cell.
source: These data suggest that Ser57 phosphorylation may regulate ubiquitin turnover in the cell since mutations that prevent or mimic phosphorylation modulate ubiquitin turnover.
evidence: This is speculation based on the effects of phosphomimetic and phospho-resistant mutations.

claim: Ser57 phosphorylation occurs at very low stoichiometry (less than 0.05% of total ubiquitin) in ppz mutant cell lysates under normal growth conditions.
source: Ser57 phosphorylation was detected in these samples but was present at a level below that required for reliable quantification – although it is clear based on internal heavy standard measurements that Ser57 phosphorylation occurs on less than 0.05% of total ubiquitin in ppz mutant cell lysates (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by MRM mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under normal growth conditions Ser57 phosphorylation occurs at very low stoichiometry and may function to regulate the turnover of a limited and/or highly localized portion of the ubiquitin pool.
source: These data suggest that under normal growth conditions Ser57 phosphorylation occurs at very low stoichiometry and may function to regulate the turnover of a limited and/or highly localized portion of the ubiquitin pool in physiological conditions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the low stoichiometry measurement.

claim: The low stoichiometry of Ser57 phosphorylation limits the ability to determine its relative contribution to overall regulation of ubiquitin homeostasis.
source: Although the rate of ubiquitin turnover is increased in ppz mutants and for Ser57Asp phosphomimetic ubiquitin, the low stoichiometry of Ser57 phosphorylation (even in ppz mutants) limits our ability to determine the relative contribution of this modification to the overall regulation of ubiquitin homeostasis.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: The Ser57Asp mutation does not cause loss of ubiquitin structure.
source: Because the Ser57Asp mutant ubiquitin retains a highly similar structure to wild-type ubiquitin (Figure 3F), we can conclude that the decreased half-life observed for Ser57Asp ubiquitin in vivo (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) is not due to disruption of ubiquitin structure.
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: The Ser57Asp mutant ubiquitin retains a highly similar structure to wild-type ubiquitin.
source: Because the Ser57Asp mutant ubiquitin retains a highly similar structure to wild-type ubiquitin (Figure 3F), we can conclude that the decreased half-life observed for Ser57Asp ubiquitin in vivo (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) is not due to disruption of ubiquitin structure.
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: The decreased half-life observed for Ser57Asp ubiquitin in vivo is not due to disruption of ubiquitin structure.
source: Because the Ser57Asp mutant ubiquitin retains a highly similar structure to wild-type ubiquitin (Figure 3F), we can conclude that the decreased half-life observed for Ser57Asp ubiquitin in vivo (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) is not due to disruption of ubiquitin structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NMR structural data.

claim: Yeast cells expressing Ser57Asp phosphomimetic ubiquitin confer resistance to canavanine.
source: Surprisingly, we found that yeast cells expressing Ser57Asp phosphomimetic ubiquitin conferred resistance to canavanine (Figure 4A and B) – indicative of a gain-of-function endocytic trafficking phenotype (Lin et al., 2008; MacGurn et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by canavanine resistance assay data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Canavanine resistance is indicative of a gain-of-function endocytic trafficking phenotype.
source: Surprisingly, we found that yeast cells expressing Ser57Asp phosphomimetic ubiquitin conferred resistance to canavanine (Figure 4A and B) – indicative of a gain-of-function endocytic trafficking phenotype (Lin et al., 2008; MacGurn et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature establishing this relationship.

claim: Mutations which prevent ubiquitin conjugation (G75V, G76V and ΔG75, ΔG76) suppress the Ser57Asp canavanine resistance phenotype.
source: Importantly, we found that mutations which prevent ubiquitin conjugation (G75V, G76V and ΔG75, ΔG76) suppressed the Ser57Asp canavanine resistance phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that conjugation is required for enhanced endocytic trafficking.
evidence: Supported by canavanine resistance assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Conjugation is required for the enhanced endocytic trafficking associated with Ser57Asp ubiquitin.
source: Importantly, we found that mutations which prevent ubiquitin conjugation (G75V, G76V and ΔG75, ΔG76) suppressed the Ser57Asp canavanine resistance phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that conjugation is required for enhanced endocytic trafficking.
evidence: This is an inference from the suppression by conjugation-defective mutations.

claim: Both K63- and K48-linked polyubiquitin are required for full canavanine resistance conferred by Ser57Asp ubiquitin.
source: Similarly, we tested if K63- or K48-linked polyubiquitin is required for the endocytic gain-of-function associated with expression of Ser57Asp phosphomimetic ubiquitin and found that both linkage types are required for full canavanine resistance (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by canavanine resistance assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The canavanine resistance phenotype caused by Ser57Asp ubiquitin requires both substrate conjugation and formation of polyubiquitin linkages.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that the canavanine resistance phenotype caused by Ser57Asp ubiquitin requires both substrate conjugation and formation of polyubiquitin linkages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the conjugation and linkage requirement experiments.

claim: Expression of Ser57Asp phosphomimetic ubiquitin results in accelerated Mup1 turnover in response to methionine addition.
source: Although the endocytosis and vacuolar degradation of Mup1 is already extremely rapid following stimulation of the cells by addition of methionine (Lin et al., 2008; MacGurn et al., 2011), we found that expression of Ser57Asp phosphomimetic ubiquitin resulted in accelerated Mup1 turnover in response to methionine addition (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by Mup1 turnover data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lower concentrations of methionine trigger rapid and efficient turnover of Mup1 in the presence of Ser57Asp phosphomimetic ubiquitin but have minimal effect in the presence of wildtype ubiquitin.
source: Furthermore, we found that lower concentrations of methionine had minimal effect on Mup1 turnover in the presence of wildtype ubiquitin but triggered rapid and efficient turnover of Mup1 in the presence of Ser57Asp phosphomimetic ubiquitin (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by Mup1-pHluorin trafficking data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Ser57Asp ubiquitin sensitizes Mup1 to endocytic trafficking and vacuolar degradation.
source: These results indicate that Ser57Asp ubiquitin sensitizes Mup1 to endocytic trafficking and vacuolar degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Mup1 trafficking experiments.

claim: Ser57 phosphorylation of ubiquitin would be sufficient to promote the trafficking of cargo to the vacuole for degradation.
source: Although these findings suggest that Ser57 phosphorylation of ubiquitin would be sufficient to promote the trafficking of cargo to the vacuole for degradation, the low stoichiometry observed for this modification (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) limits our ability to determine the relative role this modification plays in the overall regulation of endocytic trafficking.
evidence: This is speculation based on the Ser57Asp phenotypes, tempered by the low stoichiometry observation.

claim: Ser57Asp phosphomimetic mutations do not affect Rsp5 E3 ubiquitin ligase activity in vitro.
source: This analysis revealed that Ser57Asp phosphomimetic mutations do not affect Rsp5 E3 ubiquitin ligase activity in vitro (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in vitro conjugation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ser57Asp phosphomimetic ubiquitin does not exhibit altered binding to recombinant purified ESCRT-I or ESCRT-II complexes.
source: We found that Ser57Asp phosphomimetic ubiquitin did not exhibit altered binding to recombinant purified ESCRT-I or ESCRT-II complexes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), each of which contain multiple ubiquitin binding elements (Dikic et al., 2009; Shields et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fusing deubiquitylase domains to ESCRT-0 prevents cargo sorting on endosomes and delivery of cargo to the lumen of the vacuole.
source: To test this, we took advantage of the previously published observation that fusing deubiquitylase domains to ESCRT-0 prevents cargo sorting on endosomes and thus prevents delivery of cargo to the lumen of the vacuole (Stringer and Piper, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Fusing the UL36 deubiquitylase domain to Hse1 prevents delivery of Mup1 to the vacuole lumen, causing it to accumulate on the limiting membrane of the vacuole.
source: However, fusing the UL36 deubiquitylase domain to Hse1 (part of ESCRT-0) prevents delivery of Mup1 to the vacuole lumen, instead causing it to accumulate on the limiting membrane of the vacuole in response to methionine stimulation (Figure 5B, top panel).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of Ser57Asp ubiquitin facilitates bypass of the artificial DUB checkpoint created by Hse1-UL36 fusion, allowing Mup1 to traffic to the lumen of the vacuole.
source: Surprisingly, we found that expression of Ser57Asp ubiquitin facilitated bypass of this artificial DUB checkpoint, allowing Mup1 to traffic to the lumen of the vacuole (Figure 5B, bottom panel).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Fusion of Hse1 to catalytically active UL36 confers hypersensitivity to canavanine, which can be suppressed by expression of Ser57Asp ubiquitin.
source: We also observed that fusion of Hse1 to catalytically active (but not catalytically dead) UL36 conferred hypersensitivity to canavanine – consistent with a trafficking block in these strains – which could be suppressed by the expression of Ser57Asp (but not wildtype) ubiquitin (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by canavanine sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Suppression of the canavanine hypersensitive phenotype by Ser57Asp ubiquitin requires components of ESCRT-I (Vps23) and ESCRT-III (Snf7), but not components of the autophagy pathway (Atg5, Atg8).
source: Importantly, suppression of the canavanine hypersensitive phenotype by Ser57Asp ubiquitin required components of ESCRT-I (Vps23) and ESCRT-III (Snf7), but not components of the autophagy pathway (Atg5, Atg8) (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3), indicating that Ser57Asp ubiquitin restores cargo delivery to the vacuole lumen through the ESCRT pathway and not a parallel pathway.
evidence: Supported by genetic requirement data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ser57Asp ubiquitin restores cargo delivery to the vacuole lumen through the ESCRT pathway and not a parallel pathway.
source: Importantly, suppression of the canavanine hypersensitive phenotype by Ser57Asp ubiquitin required components of ESCRT-I (Vps23) and ESCRT-III (Snf7), but not components of the autophagy pathway (Atg5, Atg8) (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3), indicating that Ser57Asp ubiquitin restores cargo delivery to the vacuole lumen through the ESCRT pathway and not a parallel pathway.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic requirement data.

claim: Fusion of the arginine transporter Can1 to UL36 confers canavanine hypersensitivity that can be partially suppressed by expression of Ser57Asp ubiquitin.
source: To further test the ability of Ser57Asp ubiquitin to bypass DUB recognition, we fused the arginine transporter Can1 to UL36 and found that this also confers canavanine hypersensitivity that can be partially suppressed by expression of Ser57Asp ubiquitin (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by canavanine sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: In a cellular context, and more specifically on endosomal membranes, Ser57Asp ubiquitin bypasses DUB recognition to promote cargo trafficking to the vacuole lumen.
source: All these results indicate that in a cellular context, and more specifically on endosomal membranes, Ser57Asp ubiquitin bypasses DUB recognition in order to promote cargo trafficking to the vacuole lumen.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DUB bypass experiments.

claim: Phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of limited pools of ubiquitin localized to the endosome may impact rates of ubiquitin recycling and turnover.
source: Thus, given the low observed stoichiometry of Ser57 phosphorylation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), it is possible that phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of limited pools of ubiquitin localized to the endosome may impact rates of ubiquitin recycling and turnover.
evidence: This is speculation based on the low stoichiometry and the endosomal phenotypes.

claim: Installing the artificial DUB checkpoint significantly decreases the rate of ubiquitin degradation.
source: To test this, we measured the rate of ubiquitin degradation in strains expressing catalytically active or catalytically dead UL36 fused to Hse1 and found that installing the artificial DUB checkpoint significantly decreases the rate of ubiquitin degradation (Figure 5E, F and G).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitin turnover data shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: Expression of Ser57Asp ubiquitin increases the rate of ubiquitin degradation despite the artificial DUB checkpoint.
source: Importantly, expression of Ser57Asp ubiquitin increases the rate of ubiquitin degradation despite the artificial DUB checkpoint (Figure 5H, I and J).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitin turnover data shown in Figure 5H-J.

claim: Endosomal DUB bypass by Ser57 phosphorylated ubiquitin can regulate both endocytic trafficking and the rate of ubiquitin degradation.
source: These results illustrate how endosomal DUB bypass by Ser57 phosphorylated ubiquitin can regulate both endocytic trafficking and the rate of ubiquitin degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DUB bypass and ubiquitin turnover experiments.

claim: The Leu73Pro mutant ubiquitin, when expressed as the sole source of ubiquitin, cannot support viability.
source: Importantly, in contrast to Ser57Asp ubiquitin, the Leu73Pro mutant when expressed as the sole source of ubiquitin could not support viability (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A) – indicating that Ser57Asp mutant ubiquitin is not broadly DUB resistant.
evidence: Supported by plasmid shuffle data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Ser57Asp mutant ubiquitin is not broadly DUB resistant.
source: Importantly, in contrast to Ser57Asp ubiquitin, the Leu73Pro mutant when expressed as the sole source of ubiquitin could not support viability (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A) – indicating that Ser57Asp mutant ubiquitin is not broadly DUB resistant.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison with the Leu73Pro mutant.

claim: Exogenous expression of Leu73Pro mutant ubiquitin confers hypersensitivity to canavanine and delays Mup1 trafficking.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to Ser57Asp, exogenous expression of Leu73Pro mutant ubiquitin conferred hypersensitivity to canavanine and delayed Mup1 trafficking (Figure 5—figure supplement 5) – indicating that broad defects in deubiquitylase activity confer endocytic trafficking defects that are distinct from the endocytic gain-of-function effects observed in the presence of Ser57Asp ubiquitin.
evidence: Supported by canavanine sensitivity and Mup1 trafficking data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Broad defects in deubiquitylase activity confer endocytic trafficking defects that are distinct from the endocytic gain-of-function effects observed in the presence of Ser57Asp ubiquitin.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to Ser57Asp, exogenous expression of Leu73Pro mutant ubiquitin conferred hypersensitivity to canavanine and delayed Mup1 trafficking (Figure 5—figure supplement 5) – indicating that broad defects in deubiquitylase activity confer endocytic trafficking defects that are distinct from the endocytic gain-of-function effects observed in the presence of Ser57Asp ubiquitin.
evidence: This is an inference from the contrasting phenotypes of Leu73Pro and Ser57Asp ubiquitin.

claim: Ser57Asp does not confer broad inhibition of cellular DUB activities but rather may affect recognition by specific DUBs along the endocytic route.
source: Thus, our results suggest that Ser57Asp does not confer broad inhibition of cellular DUB activities but rather may affect recognition by specific DUBs along the endocytic route.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison with the Leu73Pro mutant.

claim: Significant Doa4 activity in vitro is only detected in the presence of Bro1.
source: As previously reported, significant Doa4 activity in vitro was only detected in the presence of Bro1 (Figure 6A), a yeast homolog of the human ALIX protein which is thought to bind and activate Doa4 on endosomes (Luhtala and Odorizzi, 2004b; Pashkova et al., 2013; Richter et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by in vitro deubiquitylation assay data shown in Figure 6A and citations to published literature.

claim: Bro1 is a yeast homolog of the human ALIX protein which is thought to bind and activate Doa4 on endosomes.
source: As previously reported, significant Doa4 activity in vitro was only detected in the presence of Bro1 (Figure 6A), a yeast homolog of the human ALIX protein which is thought to bind and activate Doa4 on endosomes (Luhtala and Odorizzi, 2004b; Pashkova et al., 2013; Richter et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Doa4 activity is significantly reduced toward Ser57Asp phosphomimetic ubiquitin.
source: Importantly, we observed that Doa4 activity was significantly reduced toward Ser57Asp phosphomimetic ubiquitin (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro deubiquitylation assay data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Ser57 phosphorylation decreases Doa4 activity toward synthetic ubiquitin.
source: We similarly tested Doa4 activity toward synthetic unmodified and Ser57 phosphorylated ubiquitin and found that Ser57 phosphorylation decreased Doa4 activity (Figure 6C, D and E).
evidence: Supported by in vitro deubiquitylation assay data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: Ser57 phosphorylation prevents ubiquitin recycling along the endocytic route by interfering with Doa4 recognition.
source: These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that Ser57 phosphorylation prevents ubiquitin recycling along the endocytic route by interfering with Doa4 recognition.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the in vitro Doa4 activity data.

claim: Δdoa4 mutant cells exhibit increased rate of ubiquitin degradation.
source: Doa4 has been reported to play an important role in ubiquitin homeostasis at least in part due to its ability to recycle ubiquitin transiting through the MVB pathway (Kimura and Tanaka, 2010; Kimura et al., 2009; Swaminathan et al., 1999), which is consistent with our finding that Δdoa4 mutant cells exhibit increased rate of ubiquitin degradation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitin turnover data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: In Δdoa4 mutant cells, Ser57Asp and Ser57Ala mutations do not modify the rate of ubiquitin turnover.
source: Importantly, in Δdoa4 mutant cells Ser57Asp and Ser57Ala mutations do not modify the rate of ubiquitin turnover (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D) – suggesting that the regulation of ubiquitin metabolism by Ser57 phosphorylation is Doa4-dependent.
evidence: Supported by ubiquitin turnover data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The regulation of ubiquitin metabolism by Ser57 phosphorylation is Doa4-dependent.
source: Importantly, in Δdoa4 mutant cells Ser57Asp and Ser57Ala mutations do not modify the rate of ubiquitin turnover (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D) – suggesting that the regulation of ubiquitin metabolism by Ser57 phosphorylation is Doa4-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of effect of Ser57 mutations in doa4 mutants.

claim: Doa4 is a major determinant of ubiquitin turnover.
source: Taken together, our results confirm the role of Doa4 as a major determinant of ubiquitin turnover and indicate that ubiquitin phosphorylation at Ser57 can facilitate bypass of Doa4, and possibly other endosomal DUB activities, to promote ubiquitin degradation by delivery to the vacuole lumen.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Doa4 experiments.

claim: Ubiquitin phosphorylation at Ser57 can facilitate bypass of Doa4, and possibly other endosomal DUB activities, to promote ubiquitin degradation by delivery to the vacuole lumen.
source: Taken together, our results confirm the role of Doa4 as a major determinant of ubiquitin turnover and indicate that ubiquitin phosphorylation at Ser57 can facilitate bypass of Doa4, and possibly other endosomal DUB activities, to promote ubiquitin degradation by delivery to the vacuole lumen.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined DUB bypass and turnover experiments.

claim: Inhibition of the proteasome has minimal effect on ubiquitin half-life in the cell, at least in the culture conditions tested.
source: To our surprise, inhibition of the proteasome had minimal affect on ubiquitin half-life in the cell, at least in the culture conditions tested (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitin turnover data with proteasome inhibitor shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Strains lacking either Pep4 or Prb1 exhibit significant stabilization of ubiquitin.
source: To test the role of vacuolar degradation in ubiquitin turnover, we measured ubiquitin half-life in a series of yeast mutants deleted for vacuolar proteases and found that strains lacking either Pep4 or Prb1 exhibited significant stabilization of ubiquitin (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitin turnover data in vacuolar protease mutants shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Most ubiquitin in the cell is degraded in the vacuole.
source: These results indicate that most ubiquitin in the cell is degraded in the vacuole.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the vacuolar protease mutant data.

claim: Deletion of Vps23 (ESCRT-I) or Snf7 (ESCRT-III) significantly abrogates ubiquitin turnover.
source: Importantly, we found that deletion of Vps23 (ESCRT-I) or Snf7 (ESCRT-III) also significantly abrogated ubiquitin turnover (Figure 7C and D, Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 3), indicating that most ubiquitin is delivered to the vacuole lumen for degradation by the MVB pathway.
evidence: Supported by ubiquitin turnover data in ESCRT mutants shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: Most ubiquitin is delivered to the vacuole lumen for degradation by the MVB pathway.
source: Importantly, we found that deletion of Vps23 (ESCRT-I) or Snf7 (ESCRT-III) also significantly abrogated ubiquitin turnover (Figure 7C and D, Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 3), indicating that most ubiquitin is delivered to the vacuole lumen for degradation by the MVB pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ESCRT mutant data.

claim: Ubiquitin accumulates primarily in the E-compartment of Δsnf7 cells.
source: In contrast, we found that ubiquitin accumulated primarily in the E-compartment (an aberrant endosomal structure) of Δsnf7 cells (Figure 7E), suggesting that a significant amount of cellular ubiquitin transits through the MVB pathway.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: A significant amount of cellular ubiquitin transits through the MVB pathway.
source: In contrast, we found that ubiquitin accumulated primarily in the E-compartment (an aberrant endosomal structure) of Δsnf7 cells (Figure 7E), suggesting that a significant amount of cellular ubiquitin transits through the MVB pathway.
evidence: This is an inference from the ubiquitin accumulation in E-compartments.

claim: Under the culture conditions tested, there is substantial ubiquitin flux through the endocytic pathway, making it an ideal point of regulation for ubiquitin degradation.
source: We conclude that – at least under the culture conditions tested in these experiments – there is substantial ubiquitin flux through the endocytic pathway, making it an ideal point of regulation for ubiquitin degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ESCRT mutant and microscopy data.

claim: Phosphorylation of ubiquitin at the Ser57 position is regulated by Ppz phosphatases in yeast.
source: Here, we report that a pair of highly similar yeast phosphatases – Ppz1 and Ppz2 – are required for proper management of ubiquitin homeostasis in yeast. We show that ppz mutants exhibit elevated levels of Ser57 phosphorylated ubiquitin – suggesting that Ser57 phosphorylation of ubiquitin may be linked to the regulation of ubiquitin homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by phosphoproteomic and immunoblot data showing elevated Ser57 phosphorylation in ppz mutants.

claim: Elevated Ser57 phosphorylation in ppz mutants contributes to ubiquitin deficiency.
source: We show that ppz mutants exhibit elevated levels of Ser57 phosphorylated ubiquitin – suggesting that Ser57 phosphorylation of ubiquitin may be linked to the regulation of ubiquitin homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by data showing partial suppression of ubiquitin deficiency by Ser57Ala mutation.

claim: Ser57 phosphorylation of ubiquitin promotes both endocytic trafficking and ubiquitin degradation.
source: We show that phosphomimetic mutations at the Ser57 position confer increased rate of ubiquitin degradation and gain-of-function endocytic trafficking phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by canavanine resistance, Mup1 trafficking, and ubiquitin turnover data.

claim: These phenotypes are associated with resistance to removal by deubiquitylases on yeast endosomes.
source: Furthermore, we present evidence that these phenotypes are associated with resistance to removal by deubiquitylases on yeast endosomes, and that this pathway plays a significant role in the regulation of ubiquitin metabolism.
evidence: Supported by in vitro Doa4 assays and DUB bypass experiments.

claim: Vacuolar degradation is the primary pathway for ubiquitin turnover in yeast cells.
source: Finally, we show that vacuolar degradation is the primary pathway for ubiquitin turnover in yeast cells, underscoring the Doa4-mediated recycling of ubiquitin as a critical point of regulation for global ubiquitin metabolism.
evidence: Supported by data showing that vacuolar protease and ESCRT mutants stabilize ubiquitin.

claim: Doa4-mediated recycling of ubiquitin is a critical point of regulation for global ubiquitin metabolism.
source: Finally, we show that vacuolar degradation is the primary pathway for ubiquitin turnover in yeast cells, underscoring the Doa4-mediated recycling of ubiquitin as a critical point of regulation for global ubiquitin metabolism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on Doa4 and ubiquitin turnover.
